source.title: Open Problems in Nuclear Density Functional Theory

accepted.question_text: In nuclear density functional theory, the Levy-Lieb energy is obtained by minimizing a density functional F[ρ] over neutron and proton densities whose integrals are fixed particle numbers N and Z, while the inner constrained search may still range over many-body density operators that are not eigenstates of the particle-number operators. A nuclear mass formula is concave when second differences of ground-state energies in the N,Z plane are positive definite. How can density functional and energy-density-functional theories, including formalisms with pairing correlations κ and particle-number fluctuation penalties, be adjusted so that the constrained minimization rigorously enforces concavity and cannot assign an ensemble density with average particle numbers N,Z an energy below the true N,Z ground-state energy?

evidence.quote: A mass formula is concave if any second difference such as, E(N + 1, Z) − 2 E(N, Z) + E(N − 1, Z), E(N, Z + 1) − 2 E(N, Z) + E(N, Z − 1), and similarly with any range in any direction of the N, Z plane, is positive definite.

Then the ensemble mixture, D = 1/2 (|ΨN+n,Z+z><ΨN+n,Z+z| + |ΨN−n,Z−z><ΨN−n,Z−z|), induces a density, 1/2 (ρN+n,Z+z + ρN−n,Z−z), with correct average particle numbers N and Z. But it returns an absurd energy, 1/2 (EN+n,Z+z + EN−n,Z−z), lower than EN,Z.
The precise adjustment of DF and EDF theories to rigorously ensure concavity is an open problem.

accepted.question_text: For a rotationally scalar nuclear Hamiltonian, the energy minimization can be restricted to scalar many-body density operators, so the associated one-body density is a radial monopole profile ρ0(r) and the resulting scalar functional is F0[ρ0]. What features of such radial density profiles determine whether the underlying nucleus is deformed, and can one formulate precise criteria, possibly using profile slopes at the nuclear surface or moments of the profiles, that distinguish spherical from deformed nuclei, hard from soft nuclei, and identify triaxial or halo nuclei?

evidence.quote: Since the energy minimization occurs within a subspace of scalar density operators, the corresponding one-body densities ρ(~r) are just radial profiles, ρ0(r). The final result is a scalar functional, F0[ρ0]. Hence an open problem : for such monopolar profiles ρ0, what is the signature for deformation? It is likely that the slope of ρ0 at the nuclear surface will be weaker for deformed nuclei than for spherical ones, but precise criteria distinguishing hard from soft nuclei are desirable, not to mention criteria identifying triaxial nuclei, halo nuclei, etc. Can one use properties of moments of the profiles?

accepted.question_text: In a radial version of nuclear Kohn-Sham density functional theory, the physical density is a scalar radial profile ρ0(r), ordinary Slater determinants built from LS orbitals |nlmσ⟩ or jj orbitals |nljm⟩ in scalar mean fields u0(r) are not themselves scalar except at subshell closure, and the proposed kinetic functional FKS0[ρ0] minimizes the kinetic energy over scalar mixtures D′0 of such determinants that reproduce ρ0. How should the Kohn-Sham procedure be adapted in this radial setting, including the construction and properties of the redefined kinetic functional FKS0[ρ0] and the radial Kohn-Sham potential uKS0(r), so that self-consistent spherical orbitals reproduce ρ0 and can be related to or compared with existing spherical and deformed nuclear energy density functionals?

evidence.quote: Another open problem consists in adapting the KS procedure to this radial world. Slater determinants, made of LS orbitals, |nlmσ>, or jj ones, |nljm>, orbitals provided by scalar mean fields u0(r), are never scalar wave functions, except at subshell closure. It seems therefore necessary to redefine the KS kinetic DF from a formula similar to Eq. (2),

Then a KS potential uKS0 can be defined as, r uKS0(r) = δ(F0 − FKS0) / r δρ0(r), and can be further simplified if a Hartree subtraction makes sense for nuclear forces. Finally a spherical set of orbitals must be generated, from the potential uKS0, to obtain self-consistency of ρ0.

Little is known at present in nuclear physics about this redefined kinetic DF, Eq. (4). It is time to import, and maybe readjust, the results that are known in atomic physics [12] [13]. While the early literature of nuclear physics is not devoid of effective spherical potentials for shell models, and while there has been recently interesting attempts to describe spherical nuclei with empirical EDFs, see for instance [14], very little is known about uKS0 either.
The program of a radial KS theory is a largely open problem.

accepted.question_text: Let Φ be a simple intrinsic nuclear state, such as a Slater determinant or Hartree-Bogoliubov state, from which rotationally projected states ΦJMK are built by angular-momentum projection. Define an intrinsic-density functional FJMK[ρ] by minimizing the projected-state energy over simple intrinsic states Φ with intrinsic density ρ; this functional depends on the allowed class of Φ and, a priori, on the angular-momentum labels J, M, and K. Under what conditions can the intrinsic state or intrinsic density be practically independent of J, M, and K so that one density ρ is valid for many projected rotational states, and how does such an intrinsic-density functional relate to the traditional three-dimensional nuclear energy density functionals used for deformed nuclei?

evidence.quote: Assume that every ΦJMK can be a good approximation to an eigenstate of H and consider the two-step minimization, EJMK = Minρ FJMK[ρ], FJMK[ρ] = MinΦ=>ρ <ΦJMK|H|ΦJMK> / <ΦJMK|ΦJMK>, where ρ is the density of Φ, and Φ is restricted to a class of simple states.
But, obviously, this DF, FJMK[ρ], depends on that subset to which Φ is restricted. Moreover, it depends on J, M, K.

But then the essentially desirable virtue of Φ would be to be practically independent of J, M, K. Can this be true? Hence the open problem : under which conditions can FJMK define just one density ρ valid for a large number of combinations JMK? How does this intrinsic DF relate [18] to the traditional three-dimensional (E)DFs used for deformed nuclei?

accepted.question_text: For electronic atoms or molecules with local Coulomb interactions, a theorem states that the square root of an eigenstate density ρ(r) obeys a one-body equation driven by a local potential usqr, with eigenvalue given by the difference between the A-particle energy and the ground-state energy of the system with one particle removed. Nuclear interactions can be strongly nonlocal, but nuclear density functional theory commonly uses local or quasi-local ingredients such as local Kohn-Sham, effective, optical, and Hartree potentials. Is there a generic approximate local potential usqr that drives √ρ and is valid for many nuclei, and if so how would it relate to nuclear density functional theory?

evidence.quote: A theorem, studied by many authors in atomic or molecular physics, see in particular [19], states that, given the density ρ(~r) of an eigenstate of H with energy EA, there exists a local potential, usqr, that drives the square root of ρ,

The theorem was established for electrons in atoms or molecules, where vij is the Coulomb repulsion, local. Locality plays a role in the proof of the theorem. It seems, therefore, that an extension of the theorem with nuclear interactions, which can be seriously non local, is excluded.

But the nuclear DFT makes an extensive use of locality or quasi-locality. The KS potential, in particular, is a functional derivative, local. Moreover, effective forces can be local, optical potentials can be local, Hartree potentials can be local, up to reasonable approximations at least. Can there be a generic form of an approximate, local usqr, valid for many nuclei? Would it relate to the nuclear DFT?

accepted.question_text: In a finite harmonic-oscillator shell-model construction, the neutron and proton densities are represented by finite density-polynomial coefficients, the Levy-Lieb density constraints and normalization constraint become algebraic polynomial equations in configuration-mixing coefficients, and eliminating constrained variables and survivor coefficients yields an implicit polynomial relation R(η, Cn1, …, CnNn, Cp1, …, CpNp) = 0 linking the minimal energy η to density parameters. What practical algebraic strategies can handle the resulting large multivariate polynomials, compare distinct polynomial relations R obtained from different finite-basis choices, extrapolate when direct calculations become too cumbersome, and make rigorous polynomial density functionals useful in larger nuclear models?

evidence.quote: One finally obtains a polynomial relation, R(η, Cn1, Cn2, ..., CnNn, Cp1, Cp2, ..., CpNp) = 0, (15) which links the minimal energy to the parameters of ρ. Although not an open formula, this implicit equation, R = 0, has all the needed virtues of a density functional for the calculation of η and its minimization in terms of the density.

It is clear that this rigorous derivation raises several technical problems, such as, for instance, the best tactics to handle big polynomials in the context of many parameters, the comparison of distinct polynomials R obtained from models with different choices for the basis, the search for extrapolations when calculations become too cumbersome. But there is no doubt that this constructive approach offers challenging open problems.

accepted.question_text: Can the algebraic polynomial construction of nuclear density functionals, which eliminates density constraints in a finite configuration-mixing model to obtain an implicit energy-density relation, also provide the Kohn-Sham potential associated with the density functional?

evidence.quote: An interesting side question arises: can this algebraic method also provide the KS potential? We have preliminary results which are optimistic, but they are only ... preliminary.

accepted.question_text: Can the same algebraic polynomial method for constructing nuclear density functionals from finite configuration-mixing models and polynomial density constraints be applied to nuclear cluster-model calculations?

evidence.quote: Another interesting question is, can this algebraic method be used for the cluster model? We have again preliminary results which are optimistic. But they are also ... too preliminary.
